extracted.intended_audience: Public water system operators, State drinking water primacy agencies, and EPA compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Requirements and standards (monitoring, sampling, treatment, corrective actions, and public notification) that public water systems using ground water must follow under Subpart S of 40 CFR Part 141 (Ground Water Rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary drinking water standards table (contaminants, MCLG, MCL, health effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of contaminants with corresponding MCLG (Maximum Contaminant Level Goal), MCL (Maximum Contaminant Level) or TT and brief health effects statements for each contaminant (including volatile organics, radioactive contaminants, disinfectant and DBP standards, and others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists contaminants (e.g., cis-1,2-dichloroethylene; trans-1,2-dichloroethylene; dichloromethane; 1,2-dichloropropane; ethylbenzene; styrene; tetrachloroethylene; toluene; 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene; 1,1,1-trichloroethane; 1,1,2-trichloroethane; trichloroethylene; vinyl chloride; xylenes (total); Beta/photon emitters; Alpha emitters; Combined radium (226 & 228); Uranium; Total trihalomethanes (TTHMs); Haloacetic Acids (HAA); Bromate; Chlorite; Chlorine; Chloramines; Chlorine dioxide; Control of DBP precursors (TOC); Acrylamide; Epichlorohydrin). For each, the table provides an MCLG and MCL (or TT, or MRDLG/MRDL), and an associated health-effects summary such as increased cancer risk, liver/kidney/nervous system effects, anemia, nervous system effects in infants/fetuses, etc. The MCLs, MRDLs, and health statements are the regulatory compliance limits and mandatory public-notification-linked health language. Examples: TTHMs MCL = 0.080 mg/L (locational running annual average); HAA5 MCL = 0.060 mg/L; Chlorine MRDL = 4.0 (MRDLG = 4). Appendix notes explain units and statutory effective dates (e.g., uranium MCL effective Dec 8, 2003).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and scope of Subpart S (Ground Water Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.400: The requirements of this subpart constitute National Primary Drinking Water Regulations and apply to all public water systems that use ground water, except systems that combine all ground water with surface water or with ground water under the direct influence of surface water prior to treatment under subpart H. 'Ground water system' includes any public water system meeting this applicability statement, including consecutive systems receiving finished ground water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General requirements listed in §141.400(c) include sanitary survey information (§141.401), microbial source water monitoring for systems that do not provide at least 4-log virus treatment (§141.402), treatment technique requirements for fecally contaminated source waters or systems with significant deficiencies (§141.403), compliance monitoring for systems providing ≥4-log virus treatment (§141.403(b)), and providing information for hydrogeologic sensitivity assessments if requested by the State. Compliance date: Ground water systems must comply beginning December 1, 2009 (unless otherwise noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary survey information requirement and components
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.401: Ground water systems must provide the State, at the State's request, any existing information that will enable the State to conduct a sanitary survey. A sanitary survey (as conducted by the State) includes an onsite review to evaluate adequacy of the system, its sources and operations and distribution of safe drinking water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sanitary survey must include evaluation of the following components: (1) Source; (2) Treatment including corrosion control treatment and water quality parameters as applicable; (3) Distribution system; (4) Finished water storage; (5) Pumps, pump facilities, and controls; (6) Monitoring, reporting, and data verification; (7) System management and operation; and (8) Operator compliance with State requirements. (§141.401(a)-(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggered source water monitoring — when required
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(a)(1): A ground water system must conduct triggered source water monitoring if the system does not provide at least 4-log treatment of viruses before or at the first customer for each ground water source and either (ii) the system is notified that a sample collected under §141.21(a) is total coliform-positive (until March 31, 2016) or (iii) is notified that a sample collected under §§141.854–141.857 is total coliform-positive (beginning April 1, 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triggered monitoring applies only to sources that lack at least 4-log virus treatment and is activated by total coliform-positive notifications as specified by the relevant monitoring provisions and dates. The 4-log treatment definition may include inactivation, removal, or a State-approved combination. (§141.402(a)(1)(i)-(iii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling requirements for triggered source water monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(a)(2): Upon notification of a total coliform-positive sample, the ground water system must collect, within 24 hours, at least one ground water source sample from each ground water source in use at the time the positive sample was collected (subject to specified exceptions and state approval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State may extend the 24-hour limit case-by-case. Systems with more than one source may, with State approval, sample representative source(s) and must submit a triggered source water monitoring plan if directed. Until March 31, 2016, ground water systems serving ≤1,000 people may use a repeat sample from a ground water source to meet both §141.21(b) and this monitoring requirement if the State approves E. coli as fecal indicator; beginning April 1, 2016 similar provisions apply under subpart Y and §141.858 with State approval. If a repeat sample is E. coli-positive, follow §141.402(a)(3). (§141.402(a)(2)(i)-(iv)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional sampling when a source sample is fecal indicator-positive
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(a)(3): If the State does not require corrective action for a fecal indicator-positive source water sample that is not invalidated, the system must collect five additional source water samples from the same source within 24 hours of being notified of the fecal indicator-positive sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement applies when the State does not direct corrective action under §141.403(a)(2) for a fecal-indicator positive sample. The five additional samples are to further assess source contamination. (§141.402(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecutive and wholesale systems: notification and downstream sampling obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(a)(4): Consecutive ground water systems that have a total coliform-positive sample must notify the wholesale system(s) within 24 hours. Wholesale systems that receive notice from a consecutive system must, within 24 hours of being notified, collect a sample from their ground water source(s) under paragraph (a)(2) and analyze it for a fecal indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the wholesale system's source sample is fecal indicator-positive, the wholesale must notify all consecutive systems served by that source within 24 hours of being notified of the result and meet the five-additional-samples requirement (§141.402(a)(3)). (§141.402(a)(4)(i)-(ii) and (a)(4)(ii)(A)-(B)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to triggered source water monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(a)(5): A ground water system is not required to comply with the triggered source water monitoring requirements if (i) the State determines and documents that the total coliform-positive sample is caused by a distribution system deficiency; or (ii) the total coliform-positive sample was collected at a location that meets State criteria for distribution system conditions that cause total coliform-positive samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State determination must be documented in writing. These exceptions permit the State to identify distribution-system causes that obviate source monitoring. (§141.402(a)(5)(i)-(ii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment source water monitoring (State-directed)
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(b): If directed by the State, ground water systems must conduct assessment source water monitoring that meets State-determined requirements. A triggered sample may be used to meet assessment monitoring requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-determined requirements may include: collection of 12 samples representing each month the system provides ground water; collection from each well unless State approves representative wells; collection of at least 100 mL standard volume for fecal indicator analysis; analysis for E. coli, enterococci, or coliphage using specified analytical methods; collection prior to any treatment unless State approves otherwise; and sample collection at the well itself unless infeasible and State approves representative location. (§141.402(b)(1)-(6)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical methods and sample handling requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(c): Ground water systems subject to source water monitoring must collect a standard sample volume of at least 100 mL for fecal indicator analysis and must analyze all source samples using one of the specified analytical methods (for E. coli, enterococci, or coliphage) or one of the alternative methods in appendix A to subpart C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable methods include: Colilert, Colisure, Membrane Filter Method with MI Agar (EPA Method 1604), m-ColiBlue24, E*Colite, EC-MUG/NA-MUG, Enterococci multiple-tube and membrane filter techniques (including EPA Method 1600), Enterolert, and coliphage methods EPA 1601/1602 (two-step enrichment and single agar layer). Time from sample collection to initiation of analysis may not exceed 30 hours; systems are encouraged but not required to hold samples below 10 °C during transit. Analyses must follow the referenced methods and incorporated documents. (§141.402(c)(1)-(2) and footnotes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidation of a fecal indicator-positive ground water source sample
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(d): A ground water system may obtain State invalidation of a fecal indicator-positive ground water source sample only if (i) the system provides the State with written notice from the laboratory that improper sample analysis occurred, or (ii) the State determines and documents in writing there is substantial evidence that the fecal indicator-positive sample is not related to source water quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the State invalidates the sample, the system must collect another source water sample under paragraph (a) within 24 hours of notification of the invalidation and have it analyzed for the same fecal indicator using the specified analytical methods. The State may extend the 24-hour limit case-by-case. (§141.402(d)(1)-(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling location requirements for source water monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(e): Any ground water source sample required under paragraph (a) must be collected at a location prior to any treatment of the ground water source unless the State approves a sampling location after treatment. If configuration does not allow sampling at the well itself, a State-approved location representative of the well's water quality may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State approval is required for after-treatment sampling locations or alternate sampling locations when well-head sampling is infeasible; the sample must be representative of the well. (§141.402(e)(1)-(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring for new ground water sources
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(f): If directed by the State, a ground water system that places a new ground water source into service after November 30, 2009 must conduct assessment source water monitoring under paragraph (b); if directed, monitoring must begin before the source is used to provide water to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State direction triggers assessment monitoring obligations for new sources; monitoring may be required prior to public use. (§141.402(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notification for fecal indicator-positive source water samples
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(g): A ground water system with a ground water source sample collected under paragraph (a) or (b) that is fecal indicator-positive and not invalidated by the State, including consecutive systems served by the ground water source, must conduct public notification under §141.202.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public notification obligations attach both to the water system with the positive source sample and to consecutive systems served by that source. The referenced §141.202 contains the required public-notification content and timing. (§141.402(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring violations and public notification
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.402(h): Failure to meet the requirements of paragraphs (a)-(f) of §141.402 is a monitoring violation and requires the ground water system to provide public notification under §141.204.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noncompliance with triggered, assessment, analytical, invalidation, sampling-location, or new-source monitoring requirements constitutes a monitoring violation subject to the public-notification procedures in §141.204. (§141.402(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment technique requirements trigger and applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.403(a)(1)-(3): Treatment technique requirements must be met by ground water systems when a significant deficiency is identified or when a ground water source sample collected under §141.402(a)(3) is fecal indicator-positive. If directed by the State, other fecal-indicator positive situations (§141.402(a)(2), (a)(4), or (b)) also trigger compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a significant deficiency is identified at a Subpart H system that uses both ground water and surface water (or ground water under the direct influence of surface water), the system must comply with the provisions of §141.403 except when the State determines the deficiency is in a portion served solely by surface water or ground water under the direct influence of surface water. Significant deficiencies include defects in design, operation, maintenance, or failures/malfunctions that the State determines are causing or could introduce contamination to consumer-delivered water. (§141.403(a)(1)-(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: State consultation timeline after notice of significant deficiency or fecal indicator-positive sample
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.403(a)(4): Unless the State directs a specific corrective action, the ground water system must consult with the State regarding appropriate corrective action within 30 days of receiving written notice from the State of a significant deficiency, written notice from a laboratory that a source sample was fecal indicator-positive, or direction from the State that a fecal indicator-positive sample requires corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consultation obligation initiates planning for corrective measures and must occur promptly (within 30 calendar days) unless the State has already directed a specific course of action. (§141.403(a)(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: 120-day corrective action completion or State-approved corrective action plan compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.403(a)(5): Within 120 days (or earlier if directed by the State) of receiving written notification of a significant deficiency, fecal indicator-positive source sample, or State direction requiring corrective action, the ground water system must either (i) have completed corrective action in accordance with applicable State plan review processes or other State guidance/direction, including State-specified interim measures; or (ii) be in compliance with a State-approved corrective action plan and schedule subject to specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions for plan compliance: any subsequent modifications to a State-approved corrective action plan and schedule must also be State-approved. If the State specifies interim measures for protecting public health pending plan approval or completion, the system must comply with those interim measures as well as the schedule. The 120-day requirement may be shortened if State directs earlier action. (§141.403(a)(5)(i)-(ii) and (a)(5)(ii)(A)-(B)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective action alternatives for systems with significant deficiencies or fecal contamination
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.403(a)(6): Ground water systems that meet the conditions triggering §141.403 must implement one or more corrective action alternatives: (i) correct all significant deficiencies; (ii) provide an alternate source of water; (iii) eliminate the source of contamination; or (iv) provide treatment that reliably achieves at least 4-log treatment of viruses before or at the first customer for the ground water source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems may implement a combination of the alternatives. The 4-log treatment can be achieved using inactivation, removal, or a State-approved combination. These alternatives are the required remediation options to protect public health in response to identified deficiencies or source contamination. (§141.403(a)(6)(i)-(iv)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special public notice for significant deficiencies or source water fecal contamination
rubrics_metrics.description: §141.403(a)(7)(i): In addition to the applicable public notification requirements of §141.202, a community ground water system that receives notice from the State of a significant deficiency or notification of a fecal indicator-positive ground water source sample that is not invalidated must provide special notice to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule requires supplemental public notification beyond §141.202 when the State notifies a community ground water system of a significant deficiency or fecal indicator-positive source sample (not invalidated). The chunked text begins this provision; full §141.403(a)(7) contains the required content and timing of the special notice. (Partial text in chunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of DBP precursors (Total Organic Carbon — TOC) as a Treatment Technique (TT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entry 93: Control of DBP precursors (TOC) — No health effects from TOC itself, but TOC provides a medium for formation of disinfection byproducts (DBPs) such as THMs and HAAs. TOC is regulated as a treatment technique (TT) rather than by an MCL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explanatory text states: 'Total organic carbon (TOC) has no health effects. However, total organic carbon provides a medium for the formation of disinfection byproducts. These byproducts include trihalomethanes (THMs) and haloacetic acids (HAAs). Drinking water containing these byproducts in excess of the MCL may lead to adverse health effects, liver or kidney problems, or nervous system effects, and may lead to an increased risk of getting cancer.' Control of TOC is therefore a preventive TT to limit DBP formation. (See §141.??? and explanatory language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chlorine dioxide exceedance public-notification addenda (treatment-facility-only vs distribution-system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add for public notification only (related to entries 91 and 92): Distinct addenda text for public notification depending on whether chlorine dioxide MRDL exceedances occurred only at the treatment facility (not in distribution system) or included exceedances within the distribution system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exceedances are at the treatment facility only: 'The chlorine dioxide violations reported today are the result of exceedances at the treatment facility only, not within the distribution system which delivers water to consumers. Continued compliance with chlorine dioxide levels within the distribution system minimizes the potential risk of these violations to consumers.' If distribution-system samples are above the MRDL: 'The chlorine dioxide violations reported today include exceedances of the EPA standard within the distribution system which delivers water to consumers. Violations of the chlorine dioxide standard within the distribution system may harm human health based on short-term exposures. Certain groups, including fetuses, infants, and young children, may be especially susceptible to nervous system effects from excessive chlorine dioxide exposure.' These are required explanatory statements to accompany public notification for chlorine dioxide MRDL exceedances. (See entries 91–92).
